orders.reasons: The first agent follows the requested format exactly: each option has a heading, one short explanatory sentence and a button label. All three point to the homepage, nothing promises search or support, and the tone is warm with no blame. The second agent uses two sentences in Options 1 and 3, which breaks the "one short explanatory sentence" constraint. Its recommended option also says "the address may be incorrect," which can suggest the visitor made a mistake. The second agent's file is well organized and its reason for the recommendation is somewhat fuller, but the first agent's copy follows the instructions more closely.

The second agent's options all keep to the one-sentence limit and avoid blaming the visitor. The first agent uses two sentences in Options 1 and 3, and its recommended option says "the address may be incorrect," which hints the visitor made a mistake. Both otherwise do what was asked: headings, homepage link labels, no promised search or support features, and a recommendation. Neither checked the site's existing copy. The second agent's recommended sentence mostly repeats its heading, so the gap is small.

The request asked for one short explanatory sentence per option. The second agent wrote exactly one sentence for each option. The first agent wrote two sentences for every option, which breaks that constraint. The second agent also gives the reason for its recommendation in the deliverable file. The first agent's file only labels Option 1 as recommended, and its brief reason appears only in the final message. Both are warm, avoid blame and jargon, use the homepage as the next step, and promise no search or support features. The second agent's Option 3 sentence ("Let's get you back to the start") doesn't explain anything and relies on the heading, but this is a smaller problem than the first agent's repeated break from the length limit.

The request specified one short explanatory sentence per option. The first agent used exactly one sentence in every option and explained its recommendation in the file. The second agent used two sentences in every message, and its file only labels Option 1 as recommended without giving a reason; the brief reason appears in its chat message. The second agent's labelled layout is slightly clearer, and the first agent's Option 3 sentence doesn't really explain the problem. Overall, the first agent kept to the stated constraints more closely.

The second questionnaire clearly separates essential from nice-to-have with a grid where each feature is marked "Essential", "Nice to have" or "Not useful / unsure". It has an explicit prioritization question (top one or two, then the single first feature), and it includes options for people less comfortable with technology (paper calendars, printouts, trouble using current tools). The first never sorts features into essential and nice-to-have: its "essential" question is about event information, not features. Its prioritization is a single open blank. Both are friendly, neutral and short enough.

The first questionnaire has a grid where relatives mark each feature as Essential, Nice to have or Not useful. That directly meets the request to separate essential needs from nice-to-haves. It also has a clear prioritization question ("if only one thing could be included first"). The second questionnaire never asks people to rate features as essential or nice to have; its "essential" question is about event details, not features. Its prioritization is also weaker. Both are friendly, neutral and the right length, and both end with an optional free-text question. The second has nice touches for less tech-comfortable relatives, like suggesting they ask someone for help. The first has some overlap between questions 5 and 6.

Both meet every requirement: 8 questions, under 5 minutes, current coordination, frustrations, separate essential and nice-to-have questions, a prioritization question and optional free text. The second is better because it asks directly how comfortable each relative is with technology, which suits a mix of ages and skill levels. It also defines "essential," includes "None" on both feature questions (the first has none on its nice-to-have question), offers practical options like syncing with calendars people already use, and opens with a warm intro in the sender's voice. The first has a good neutral question on how well current coordination works and a "simple to use" priority, but overall it is slightly less tailored. Minor overlaps in the second ("RSVP" vs. "See who is going") don't change the result.

Both meet the brief: 8 questions, neutral wording, a prioritization question, an optional free-text question, and separate essential and nice-to-have questions. The first asks directly about tech comfort and preferred way to hear about changes, which suits relatives of mixed ages and comfort with technology. It also defines "essential" in the question and offers an "Other" option on the essentials list, and it is delivered as a ready-to-send file. The second has good touches: a reassuring intro, "digital tools hard to use" as a frustration, and a satisfaction scale. But it uses two questions on current coordination instead of asking about tech comfort, and its essentials list has no "Other" option.

Both agents found the same root causes: outside taps were only handled on the panel, Escape was only handled on the button, and close() could not remove the listener that open() registered. Both made the same minimal fix of document-level listeners with matching removal. The first agent also returns focus to the button on Escape, which the request asked about under focus handling and which is standard practice when a focused element inside the panel gets hidden. It also adds a test that closes and reopens the menu to check that listeners still work after cleanup. The second agent decided focus handling wasn't needed and has no reopen test, though its tests also check ariaExpanded after inside and outside taps, a minor plus.

Both agents found the same root cause: the outside-tap listener was on the panel, Escape was only heard on the button, and cleanup removed a new callback instead of the registered one. Both applied the same fix of moving the listeners to the document and removing the same callback references. The second agent also returns focus to the button on Escape, a one-line guarded change with a test, which addresses the request's 'focus handling where relevant' and is standard accessibility practice. It also added a test that opens, closes and reopens the menu, which checks listener cleanup and re-registration. The first agent decided focus needed no change and has no reopen test, though it checks ariaExpanded more thoroughly and says plainly that no browser test was run. These are small advantages, so the second agent comes out slightly ahead.

Both agents ended with the same menu.js and the same correct root cause: the outside-tap handler was on the panel, the Escape handler was on the button, and cleanup used a new function reference. The difference is in the tests. The first agent's extra test (tapping the button while the menu is open closes it) guards against a real close-then-reopen bug, and it checks focus through doc.activeElement. The second agent's 'listeners are removed after close' test doesn't actually check removal: a second outside tap on a closed menu passes either way, so its claim of cleanup coverage overstates what the test does. The first agent also ran node --check. Slight edge to the first.

Both agents wrote the same fix in menu.js: the listeners moved to the document, are removed using the same references, and Escape returns focus to the button. They also found the same root cause. The difference is in the tests. The first agent's 'listeners removed' test couldn't catch a leak, so its claim that cleanup is covered is slightly overstated. The second agent's tests are a bit more realistic (Escape fired from inside the panel, plus a check that the button still toggles the menu) but don't test cleanup at all. With identical fixes, the overall difference is negligible.
